author: From Staff Reports
title: Braxton County: Hot spot for freshwater anglers | News | wvnews.com
text:
SUTTON, W.Va. — Known as the "Geographic Center of West Virginia," Braxton County has solidified its reputation in 2026 as a premier destination for freshwater anglers, anchored by two massive reservoirs and a river system teeming with biological diversity.
From the muskie-rich waters of Burnsville Lake to the high-yield bass populations of Sutton Lake and the cold-water trout runs of the Elk and Holly rivers, the county offers a trifecta of fishing environments within a 30-minute drive of Interstate 79.
According to data from the West Virginia Division of Natural Resources (WVDNR) and the Elk River Water Trail, these waterways remain some of the most productive in the state for both recreational family outings and professional-grade sport fishing.
Braxton County is unique in that it houses two of West Virginia’s largest flood-control reservoirs, both managed by the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers.
Sutton Lake, a 1,500-acre impoundment, serves as the county's primary hub for bass anglers.
A recent sport fish stock assessment by fisheries biologists revealed a dynamic population of largemouth, smallmouth, and spotted bass.
Recent electrofishing surveys documented over 500 largemouth bass per sampling session, with growth rates exceeding state averages due to the lake's rich forage base.
The primary species found here include largemouth bass, smallmouth bass, spotted bass, and crappie.
Top spots for these species include the Bee Run area and the waters surrounding the Sutton Dam tailwaters.
WVDNR reports for 2026 indicate that mid-depth drop-shot rigs and tube baits are currently the most effective for the lake's spotted bass population, which tends to congregate around submerged rocky structures.
Located just north of Sutton, the 968-acre Burnsville Lake is widely recognized as one of the best muskellunge (muskie) fisheries in the Eastern United States.
In addition to muskie, the lake is a stronghold for channel catfish and crappie.
The primary species of interest are muskellunge, channel catfish, largemouth bass, and flathead catfish.
The Bulltown Campground and Riffle Run boat ramps provide the primary access points for boaters.
According to 2026 fishing reports, Burnsville’s water temperature averages 60°F in early spring, creating excellent conditions for cool-water species like walleye.
This lake remains a cornerstone for those seeking the "fish of ten thousand casts," with the WVDNR continuing its aggressive muskie stocking program to ensure high catch rates.
The Elk River is often heralded by the Braxton County Convention and Visitors Bureau as the best all-in-one river in West Virginia.
This is not hyperbole; the river’s tailwaters below the Sutton Dam provide a unique thermal environment that supports both cold-water trout and warm-water game fish.
The Elk River Water Trail begins at the Sutton Dam tailwaters and flows through the heart of the county. This section is considered a biological treasure, home to rare invertebrates and a staggering variety of fish.
Trout are found most consistently immediately below the Sutton Dam in the tailwaters, while smallmouth bass thrive in the mid-river sections near Gassaway.
Muskellunge are often found in the deep pools between Frametown and the Clay County line, and walleye frequent the fast-moving runs near rocky outcrops.
For those seeking a more secluded experience, the Holly River offers a different pace.
The river is the shortest in West Virginia, flowing only 3 miles before entering Sutton Lake, but its impact on the local ecosystem is significant.
The Left Fork of the Holly River is a designated trout stream, frequently stocked by the WVDNR.
Anglers at Holly River typically target brook trout and black bullhead. The Right Fork is also a favorite for those using light tackle for bluegill and smallmouth bass.
This area is particularly popular for fly fishing enthusiasts who prefer the smaller, more intimate water settings compared to the vast expanse of the county's reservoirs.
The WVDNR 2026 Fishing Regulations Summary emphasizes several key rules for Braxton County waters to maintain the health of these fisheries.
Specific sections of the Elk River may be subject to catch-and-release only for certain species, and anglers are encouraged to consult the 2026 WVDNR map for precise boundaries.
Boating safety is also a priority; anyone born after Dec. 31, 1986, must complete a boating education course before operating a motorboat on Sutton or Burnsville lakes.
Furthermore, to protect the biological treasure of the Elk River, the WVDNR strictly prohibits moving live fish or bait between different bodies of water to prevent the spread of invasive species.
Access to these locations is facilitated by well-maintained infrastructure.
Sutton Lake is best accessed via the Bee Run Recreation Area near the town of Sutton, while Burnsville Lake is served by Riffle Run and Bulltown.
The Elk River features multiple entry points, including the Gassaway Marina and the tailwaters area. The Holly River is easily reached via Holly River State Park or the northern reaches of Sutton Lake.

According to data from the West Virginia Division of Natural Resources (WVDNR) and the Elk River Water Trail, these waterways remain some of the most productive in the state for both recreational family outings and professional-grade sport fishing.
